Addressable Memory for Video World Models

Xindi Wu1 2 Sven Elflein1 3 4 James Lucas1 Olga Russakovsky2 Laura Leal-Taixé1 Despoina Paschalidou1 Jonathan Lorraine1 Aljosa Osep1
1NVIDIA  2Princeton University  3University of Toronto  4Vector Institute
https://research.nvidia.com/labs/sil/projects/WorldTrace/
Abstract

We study visual persistence in interactive video world models. These models rely on a Key-Value (KV) cache as a growing visual memory to carry forward previously generated frames. However, we find that models can no longer reliably address stored content once rollouts extend beyond the training horizon, because temporal Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE) offsets then fall outside the range seen during training and the model struggles to retrieve the relevant visual information through attention. Moreover, naively compressing the cache in the RoPE-rotated space corrupt memory by averaging together incompatible positional phases. To address this, we propose WorldTrace, a training-free memory framework for long-horizon visual persistence. WorldTrace keeps compressed memory addressable by assigning each summary slot a distinct, in-distribution virtual position. Within this addressable cache, we study two memory compression approaches: WorldTrace-Field compresses history for temporal coherence, while WorldTrace-Landmark stores verbatim scene traces at detected transitions for episodic recall. We further introduce LoopBench, a benchmark evaluating whether a compressed cache can reconstruct a previously visited scene after a long detour. WorldTrace-Field improves temporal consistency by +15.5%, and WorldTrace-Landmark improves episodic recall by +19.5% on LoopBench, extending visually persistent generation without retraining.

\abscontent

1 Introduction

Memory is what makes a generated world persistent. A world model should not only predict what comes next, but also preserve what has already been seen. World models aim to simulate worlds we can explore [29, 30, 25], and recent autoregressive video world models [82, 32, 20] pursue this vision by generating video scenes chunk-by-chunk, with each chunk attending over a Key-Value (KV) cache of prior context. These models promise interactive applications such as next-generation game engines [84, 20, 32] and closed-loop robot simulators [1, 3], in which users can move freely through a visual world and revisit prior locations. Such revisits demand visual persistence, meaning that when an agent returns, the generated results should be consistent with the scene’s original appearance, not a plausible-looking alternative.

In practice, visual persistence degrades rapidly once generation exceeds the training context length. A natural way to address this issue is to compress the linearly growing KV cache into a fixed-size memory [115, 53, 9, 42] equal to the size of the context seen during training. However, we find that the bottleneck is not simply whether past content is stored in the cache, but whether it remains addressable and how it is compressed. As the generation horizon extends beyond the training context length, the positional encoding these models rely on (e.g., RoPE [78]) is queried at position indices outside its training-bounded range, so the model needs to attend over relative distances that are out-of-distribution (OOD), degrading attention-based memory retrieval. In other words, even if past memories are stored in the KV cache, the model cannot reliably retrieve them. A summary placed at such an offset can therefore become hard to reach. This reveals that long-horizon failure is fundamentally a problem of addressability, since no memory scheme can improve visual persistence if past observations cannot be reliably accessed once they fall outside the context window.

WorldTrace.

To tackle this problem, we propose WorldTrace, a training-free approach for addressable compressed memory over long horizons. We assign each memory entry a fixed, in-distribution temporal position relative to the current frame, keeping past observations within the temporal positional encoding range the model was trained on so that distant tokens remain retrievable. The cache is organized into a recent window and summary slots for the distant horizon. Within this addressable cache, the remaining challenge is what the world model should choose to remember. We view this as a structured projection of a growing visual history into a fixed set of retrievable traces. We propose two complementary memory writers: WorldTrace-Field which preserves the coarse field of past information in rotation-invariant space for temporal coherence, and WorldTrace-Landmark which preserves sparse scene-entry traces for long-horizon recall.

Our experiments show that addressable memory extends the effective memory horizon. To evaluate episodic recall under controlled scene revisits, we propose LoopBench, a memory benchmark that tests whether the compressed KV cache can retrieve a previously visited scene after a long detour. While the sliding-window baseline begins to forget scene structure after only a few seconds and loses structural fidelity when revisiting the same location, our WorldTrace maintains consistent scene reconstruction over long rollouts and recovers the original scene appearance (Fig. 1).

Our contributions are:

  1. 1.

    We identify two coupled challenges for long-horizon generation in autoregressive video world models, where memory is placed and what it stores. Out-of-distribution temporal offsets make cached tokens hard to address, and RoPE phase cancellation makes naively compressed summaries uninformative (Sec. 2).

  2. 2.

    We propose WorldTrace, a training-free approach that keeps compressed memory both addressable and useful without retraining. It assigns each summary an in-distribution virtual position (Sec. 3.1) and organizes the growing visual history into a fixed set of retrievable traces, realized by two complementary operators: WorldTrace-Field for temporal coherence (Sec. 3.3) and WorldTrace-Landmark for episodic recall (Sec. 3.4).

  3. 3.

    We introduce LoopBench, a memory benchmark of controlled scene revisits that measures whether a compressed cache can recover a previously visited scene (Sec. 4). We show that WorldTrace extends the effective memory horizon over the default sliding-window cache, with WorldTrace-Field improving temporal consistency by +15.5% on long rollouts and WorldTrace-Landmark improving episodic recall by +19.5% on LoopBench ABA revisits, both without retraining.

2 Rethinking Memory in Video World Models

Autoregressive video world models retain prior context as cached keys and values during generation. Long-horizon memory therefore depends both on whether relevant past context remains inside the cache and on whether the model can effectively attend to it during future generation. Two coupled bottlenecks arise. First, cached tokens need to remain addressable (Sec. 2.1), because attending to a distant token requires a temporal RoPE offset that may lie outside the training distribution, which leaves the token unreadable even when stored. Second, compressed summaries need to remain informative (Sec. 2.2), because naively compressing old keys lets mismatched RoPE phases cancel out the signal the summary is supposed to carry.

2.1 Position Determines Whether Memory Is Addressable

A cached token helps only if the current query can still attend to it. Because a token’s temporal RoPE offset from the current query grows with how far back it lies, entries eventually carry offsets beyond the range seen during training, at which point the model can no longer read them even though they still sit in the cache. We summarize the notations in App. A.

Concretely, during training the query only attends over a bounded range of relative offsets δq,k\smash{\delta_{q,k}} between the current frame and each cached frame:

0≤δq,k=q−k≤Δ​ttrain,0\leq\smash{\delta_{q,k}}=q-k\leq\smash{\Delta t_{\mathrm{train}}},

where qq is the absolute position of the current query frame, kk that of a cached key frame, with k≤qk\leq q under causal autoregressive attention, and Δ​ttrain\smash{\Delta t_{\mathrm{train}}} the largest offset seen during training.

For temporal RoPE pair ff at angular frequency θf\smash{\theta_{f}}, its contribution aq,kf\smash{a_{q,k}^{f}} to the query-key attention score is:

aq,kf=Re⁡(Aq,kf​ei​θf​δq,k),\smash{a_{q,k}^{f}}=\mathrm{Re}\!\left(\smash{A_{q,k}^{f}}e^{i\smash{\theta_{f}}\smash{\delta_{q,k}}}\right),

where Re⁡(⋅)\mathrm{Re}(\cdot) is the real part and Aq,kf\smash{A_{q,k}^{f}} is the content-dependent inner product in canonical coordinates between the query at qq and the key at kk. During long-horizon inference, these offsets grow ever larger, and δq,k\smash{\delta_{q,k}} can exceed Δ​ttrain\smash{\Delta t_{\mathrm{train}}}. The affected RoPE components then take on rotation angles the model never saw during training. This effect is frequency-dependent, with the fastest temporal components degrading into positional noise while slower ones stay close to their trained range and keep carrying usable signal [67, 2]. We quantify this per frequency in App. C.

Several concurrent methods investigate related positional issues. Infinity-RoPE [107] proposes Block-relative RoPE which reindexes each cached frame relative to the current AR chunk so that δq,k\smash{\delta_{q,k}} always stays within the trained range, keeping generation in-distribution without a fixed memory budget. It targets infinite video generation rather than memory compression. Applied to a compressed cache, however, this reindexing caps every offset at Δ​ttrain\smash{\Delta t_{\mathrm{train}}}, so distinct summary slots collapse onto the same position and become indistinguishable (Rem. 1). MemRoPE [42] compresses history into two EMA memory tokens, a long-term and a short-term stream, which avoids this collapse simply because only two summaries need distinct positions. The design is fixed to two streams and does not extend to an NN-slot cache, where capped Block-relative positions would again collide. Unlike these, our WorldTrace targets an NN-slot compressed cache directly by assigning every slot a distinct, in-distribution slot-rank position, so an arbitrary number of summaries stay individually addressable at any horizon. We provide a detailed discussion of related work in App. D.

2.2 Content Compression Determines Whether Memory Is Informative

Even a summary placed at an in-distribution temporal position is only worth reading if compression preserved what it encodes. A common way to compress cached keys is averaging [6, 71]. With RoPE-rotated keys, at frequency ff this corresponds to:

K¯naivef=1M​∑m=1MR⁡(θf​tm)​Kmf,\smash{\bar{K}_{\mathrm{naive}}^{f}}=\smash{\frac{1}{M}}\sum\nolimits_{m=1}^{M}R\!\left(\smash{\theta_{f}}t_{m}\right)\,\smash{K_{m}^{f}},

where Kmf\smash{K_{m}^{f}} is the canonical (unrotated) key of frame mm at frequency ff and R⁡(θf​tm)R\!\left(\smash{\theta_{f}}t_{m}\right) is its RoPE rotation. Each frame is rotated by a different angle θf​tm\smash{\theta_{f}}t_{m} before averaging, so K¯naivef\smash{\bar{K}_{\mathrm{naive}}^{f}} sums vectors that point in different directions. If the frames come from nearby timestamps, their rotation angles are close, so averaging largely preserves the signal. If they come from distant timestamps, their angles can point in opposite directions and partially cancel, weakening that frequency’s contribution to the summary regardless of what it encoded. Naive averaging in RoPE-rotated space thus corrupts the compressed memory.

The two failures are coupled.

Most prior methods fix only one of the two, with one line of work adjusting where memories are placed, reparameterizing or capping offsets (\egBlock-relative [107]), while another decides what each summary stores, whether by smoothing past keys with dual-rate EMA [42], merging them by temporal averaging [6, 71], or evicting entries [115, 53, 9]. Addressable positions cannot help if compression cancels the signal a summary should carry, and an informative summary cannot help if it sits at an out-of-distribution position. Thus we need to keep compressed memory both addressable and informative once generation exceeds the training window. Visual persistence in a video world model demands exactly this, because an agent that explores and later revisits a location needs the cache to keep those distant scenes readable across long detours (addressability) and to retain enough of their content to regenerate them faithfully (informativeness). Our WorldTrace is built to satisfy both, which is what lets a generated world stay consistent over long, interactive rollouts.

3 WorldTrace

We propose WorldTrace, a training-free approach for addressable memory in autoregressive video world models. WorldTrace maintains a bounded trace of distant history in fixed summary slots via canonical-space key assignment, while keeping each slot addressable (Sec. 3.1). We formulate this cached memory compression for visual persistence as structured sparse attention (Sec. 3.2, App. B). Its two variants, WorldTrace-Field (Sec. 3.3) and WorldTrace-Landmark (Sec. 3.4), target temporal coherence and episodic recall, respectively.

3.1 Virtual Position Assignment: WorldTrace Slot Indexing

Cache structure.

As shown in Fig. 2, we partition the local attention window Lattn\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}} into a recent window ℛ\mathcal{R} of Nr\smash{N_{r}} verbatim latent frames and a summary cache 𝒮\mathcal{S} of Ns\smash{N_{s}} slots storing compressed history, so that Ns+Nr=Lattn\smash{N_{s}}+\smash{N_{r}}=\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}}.

Given this cache structure, the remaining question is how to position each summary slot relative to the query. A memory position scheme assigns a virtual position to summary slot ss for a query at timestamp qq, and to be usable by the attention mechanism, it should satisfy four properties: (i) linearity in qq and ss for a simple predictable mapping, (ii) in-distribution positions so the model can attend, (iii) horizon-stability so virtual positions stay in-distribution at any generation length, and (iv) distinct positions for each slot so attention can tell them apart. Summary slot positions must stay within the range seen during training:

tminv=max⁡(0,q−Δ​ttrain),tmaxv=q−Nr.\smash{t_{\min}^{v}}=\max\!\bigl(0,\;q-\smash{\Delta t_{\mathrm{train}}}\bigr),\quad\smash{t_{\max}^{v}}=q-\smash{N_{r}}. (1)

Within those bounds, each summary slot takes the position fixed by its rank.

Definition 1 (WorldTrace Slot Indexing).

Given current query position qq, local attention window Lattn\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}} (=Ns+Nr=\smash{N_{s}}+\smash{N_{r}}), and summary cache size Ns\smash{N_{s}}, the virtual position of summary slot ss is:

tsv=q−(Lattn−1−s),s=0,…,Ns−1.\smash{t_{s}^{v}}\;=\;q-(\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}}{-}1{-}s),\quad s=0,\ldots,\smash{N_{s}}{-}1. (2)

The assignment covers the in-distribution range with fixed slot-rank offsets relative to the current frame. By construction, tsv∈[tminv,tmaxv]\smash{t_{s}^{v}}\in[\smash{t_{\min}^{v}},\smash{t_{\max}^{v}}] at any generation length, offsets depend only on slot rank and qq, and importantly, not the absolute horizon NN.

Remark 1 (Block-relative collapse).

Block-relative positions [107] cap all KV-cache offsets at Δ​ttrain\smash{\Delta t_{\mathrm{train}}} (Sec. 2.1). As generation grows, summary slots spanning history beyond Δ​ttrain\smash{\Delta t_{\mathrm{train}}} steps back all share the same minimum virtual position tminv\smash{t_{\min}^{v}}, making the compressed slots positionally indistinguishable. Our WorldTrace slot indexing (Def. 1) avoids this by anchoring each virtual position to slot rank through tsv=q−(Lattn−1−s)\smash{t_{s}^{v}}{=}q{-}(\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}}{-}1{-}s), whose offset (Lattn−1−s)(\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}}{-}1{-}s) is fixed by slot rank alone and therefore keeps all Ns\smash{N_{s}} slots distinct at any generation horizon NN.

Why canonical keys.

Each slot’s virtual position tsv\smash{t_{s}^{v}} is set by slot rank (Def. 1), independently of the original timestamps {tm}\{t_{m}\} of its source frames, so placing compressed content at tsv\smash{t_{s}^{v}} requires first unrotating each key to remove its original RoPE rotation and then re-rotating to the target phase at tsv\smash{t_{s}^{v}}. Compressing in the rotated domain fails for two reasons: keys carrying distinct rotations R⁡(θf​tm)R\!\left(\smash{\theta_{f}}t_{m}\right) point in different directions at each frequency and partially cancel when combined, and the compressed key would still carry the phase of its source timestamps rather than that of tsv\smash{t_{s}^{v}}. Storing keys canonically resolves both. Concurrent memory-token work adopts the same mechanism [42] and what we add is its pairing with slot-rank positions (Def. 1). With addressable summary slots, the remaining design choice is the content writer. Both WorldTrace variants use the same canonical (un-rotated) key domain.

3.2 Memory Compression as Structured Sparse Attention

With slot positions fixed, the remaining choice is what to store in each slot. A bounded cache can take neither extreme, since storing all past frames verbatim would let the KV cache grow linearly with generation length, while evicting them, as a sliding window does, is precisely what destroys visual persistence (Sec. 2). What remains is to compress distant history rather than discard it. We view this memory compression as structured sparse attention because that view states the design target explicitly, asking the compressed cache to approximate full attention over all TT past frames with a fixed-LL structured sparse pattern in which each of the LL cache slots summarizes a segment of the full history. Framing the problem this way turns the choice of slot content into a quantifiable approximation problem. The projection matrix P∈ℝL×TP\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times T} defines this pattern by giving slot ii the compressed key Pi​KmfP_{i}\smash{K_{m}^{f}}, rotated to the slot’s virtual position. The recent window uses verbatim identity rows for the last Nr\smash{N_{r}} frames, and the Ns\smash{N_{s}} summary rows carry the compressed information.

Approximating full attention.

Attending over all TT past frames would produce a softmax-weighted combination of their values, with weights αq\alpha_{q} determined by query-key similarity. In order to keep the cache bounded, memory compression replaces this with projected attention over LL compressed keys, where row ii of PP defines which past frames contribute to compressed key ii, given by Pi​KmfP_{i}\smash{K_{m}^{f}}. Re-encoding each compressed key at tsv\smash{t_{s}^{v}} keeps the approximation in-distribution at any horizon. We approximate the error with the distribution mismatch between the full attention weights αq\alpha_{q} and the weights induced by the compressed cache (Prop. 1, App. B). The choice of PP therefore determines which parts of history are preserved under a fixed slot budget.

Choosing the projection matrix.

This view reduces memory compression design to the choice of PP, with a good PP minimizing the distribution mismatch above for the queries encountered during rollout. Relaxing the entries of PP from fixed patterns to arbitrary nonnegative values turns this minimization into a nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF) problem [44], approximately factoring the matrix of full attention weights into the product of two nonnegative low-rank factors (App. B). The optimal row structure of PP then depends on these queries. Near-optimal rows average contiguous temporal groups when future attention spreads smoothly over history, and select single frames verbatim when it concentrates instead on a few salient past frames. These two attention patterns motivate the two variants we introduce next, WorldTrace-Field (Sec. 3.3) and WorldTrace-Landmark (Sec. 3.4).

3.3 WorldTrace-Field: Canonical Key Averaging

In order to maintain temporal coherence when future attention spreads smoothly over history, we propose WorldTrace-Field, which instantiates the averaging case of Sec. 3.2 by having each summary row of PP uniformly average the contiguous temporal group of frames assigned to its slot, compressing distant history into rotation-invariant slot traces. To avoid the phase-cancellation failure mentioned in Sec. 2.2, we fix the compression domain by aligning all source keys to a shared phase before averaging, i.e., the canonical (unrotated) representation:

Definition 2 (Canonical Key Averaging (WorldTrace-Field operator)).

For each temporal head-dimension pair ff, the compressed key at virtual position tvt^{v} is:

Kfieldf​(tv)=R⁡(θf​tv)​1M​∑m=1MR⁡(−θf​tm)​Ktmf,{K}_{\mathrm{field}}^{f}\!\left(t^{v}\right)\;=\;R\!\left(\smash{\theta_{f}}t^{v}\right)\,\smash{\frac{1}{M}}\sum\nolimits_{m=1}^{M}R\!\left(-\smash{\theta_{f}}t_{m}\right)\,\smash{K_{t_{m}}^{f}}, (3)
\ie

we unrotate each key to its canonical content R⁡(−θf​tm)​KtmfR\!\left(-\smash{\theta_{f}}t_{m}\right)\,\smash{K_{t_{m}}^{f}}, average in that space, and then re-encode at virtual position tvt^{v}. Values are not rotated, as only keys carry RoPE. Slot values are computed as the mean of the source-frame values assigned to the slot. The count MM follows from the grouping rather than being a separate hyperparameter. The T−NrT{-}\smash{N_{r}} frames that have left the recent window are split into Ns\smash{N_{s}} contiguous temporal groups (oldest to newest, slot ss receives group ss), giving M≈T/NsM\approx T/\smash{N_{s}} per slot, a ratio that grows linearly with generation length NN.

Every new chunk pushes another frame out of the recent window and changes which frames each group covers, so the slot averages have to be maintained as the rollout grows. Frames are never averaged away irreversibly. The writer keeps the canonical key of each evicted frame in host memory and recomputes every slot mean from its own source set at each step, so a moving boundary always acts on source frames and never on an already averaged quantity. Peak GPU memory therefore stays equal to the sliding-window baseline because the retained keys live outside the cache (App. E.6).

Remark 2 (Mean attention preservation, informal).

Since a summary slot stands in for its MM source frames, a query should attend to it roughly as it would have attended to those frames, which makes any compression that silently changes these attention scores a source of bias toward or away from distant history. Def. 2 provides exactly this guarantee by constructing a compressed key that preserves the mean attention score the source keys {Ktmf}m=1M\{\smash{K_{t_{m}}^{f}}\}_{m=1}^{M} would receive if each were reassigned the shared virtual position tvt^{v} (formal statement in App. C, Prop. 2). Averaging in the rotated domain offers no such guarantee, as phase cancellation shrinks the compressed key and suppresses the score (Sec. 2.2). The guarantee is stated on pre-softmax scores, and it does not extend to the weights themselves, since after softmax each attention weight also depends on every other cached key.

3.4 WorldTrace-Landmark: Landmark Traces with Frozen Keys

To optimize for episodic recall, WorldTrace-Landmark fills the Ns\smash{N_{s}} slots with verbatim high-value past frames rather than averaged summaries. This is akin to Landmark Attention [63]. However, unlike token-level landmark insertion in trained transformers, our method uses scene-entry detection, frozen canonical keys, and slot-rank virtual positions.

Landmark selection.

We identify recall-relevant frames from the canonical-K representation of Eq. (3), computing for each incoming frame the cosine distance between the canonical keys of consecutive frames and marking any frame whose distance spikes above threshold τ\tau as a scene-entry event. WorldTrace-Landmark fills the Ns\smash{N_{s}} summary slots with the most recent scene-entry frames verbatim, and while fewer than Ns\smash{N_{s}} scene-entry events have been detected, the remaining slots repeat the oldest available landmark. Once more than Ns\smash{N_{s}} scene-entry events have been detected over a long rollout, the oldest is evicted to make room for the newest. Landmark slots use the same position assignment as Eq. (2), so each landmark frame inherits the slot-rank position of its summary slot rather than its absolute timestamp.

Frozen landmark keys.

Slots are ordered from oldest (s=0s{=}0) to newest, so each new chunk shifts every cached frame one slot toward the older end, moving a landmark frame from slot ss at chunk nn to slot s−1s{-}1 at chunk n+1n{+}1. Under standard summary updates, each shift unrotates the cached Key to its canonical form, then re-rotates it to its new virtual position. Over many shifts, these unrotate-rerotate cycles accumulate floating-point errors. This is exacerbated in practice by bfloat16 precision, as shown by Wang et al. [88]. WorldTrace-Landmark removes this drift by freezing each selected key in canonical form, storing that key once at landmark time and applying a single fresh rotation to the current virtual position at every subsequent shift:

Klandf​(tsv)=R⁡(θf​tsv)​R​(−θf​tℓ∗)​Ktℓ∗f,{K}_{\mathrm{land}}^{f}\!\left(\smash{t_{s}^{v}}\right)\;=\;R\!\left(\smash{\theta_{f}}\smash{t_{s}^{v}}\right)\,R\!\left(-\smash{\theta_{f}}\smash{t_{\ell^{*}}}\right)\,\smash{K_{\smash{t_{\ell^{*}}}}^{f}}, (4)

where tℓ∗\smash{t_{\ell^{*}}} is the original timestamp of the selected landmark frame. Compared to Eq. (3), the form is identical (unrotate to canonical, re-rotate to virtual position), with M=1M{=}1 and no averaging. The canonical key R⁡(−θf​tℓ∗)​Ktℓ∗fR\!\left(-\smash{\theta_{f}}\smash{t_{\ell^{*}}}\right)\,\smash{K_{\smash{t_{\ell^{*}}}}^{f}} is computed once at landmark time and reused across all subsequent shifts. The canonical-caching mechanism is shared with concurrent work that stores RoPE keys canonically and rotates at attention time (\egMemRoPE [42]). WorldTrace-Landmark differs in (i) applying it selectively at detected scene-entry events rather than to every cached key, and (ii) combining it with the slot-rank position assignment, so each frozen landmark occupies a distinct in-distribution virtual position at any horizon.

A unified view.

Viewed through the structured sparse attention lens in Sec. 3.2, WorldTrace-Field and WorldTrace-Landmark differ only in the choice of the projection matrix PP, each matched to a family of future queries. Under WorldTrace-Field (Sec. 3.3), each summary row uniformly averages keys over a disjoint temporal group, yielding exactly the canonical key averaging of Eq. (3). This is near-optimal when attention varies smoothly within each compressed slot, so that future queries care about group-level history rather than individual frame identity (Eq. (6), App. B). Under WorldTrace-Landmark, each summary row instead selects a single detected scene-entry frame verbatim, recovering its frozen canonical key as in Eq. (4). This is near-optimal when recall queries concentrate on a small set of salient past scenes (Eq. (8), App. B). Together the two variants cover the query families that dominate long-horizon rollouts, smooth continuation and episodic recall, and both realize the same slot-rank, canonical-store design, differing only in the rows of PP.

3.5 Position-Content Coupling

As noted in Sec. 2, position assignment and content compression are coupled. Concretely, the virtual positions assigned to summary slots can diverge from the offset range under which their keys were compressed, so the cached content may no longer match what the query attends to. Block-relative collapse makes compressed entries effectively unaddressable, reducing compression to sliding-window eviction once addressability collapses (Rem. 1). Averaging position-conditioned keys under one offset distribution and querying them under another changes the effective phase of cached tokens, breaking the mean-attention preservation that motivates Def. 2.

WorldTrace resolves this coupling by combining two mechanisms. Slot indexing (Def. 1) fixes a consistent virtual position scheme, while canonical key averaging (WorldTrace-Field) and frozen landmark keys (WorldTrace-Landmark) absorb the source-to-virtual shift by unrotating keys to canonical space and re-encoding at slot-rank positions. Within this framework, the choice of slot content, averaged frames or frozen landmarks, becomes a content-only design choice. We provide the detailed algorithm in App. G.

4 Experiments

We organize our experiments around our three claims. (Q1, Sec. 4.2) Is position, not content, the binding constraint? (Q2, Sec. 4.2) Does WorldTrace-Field improve coherence over naive averaging and a sliding-window cache? (Q3, Sec. 4.3) Can WorldTrace-Landmark improve episodic recall at extended horizons?

4.1 Setup

Models.

Our evaluation uses Matrix-Game-2 (MG2-1.3B) [32], a distilled 1.3B-parameter autoregressive game world model based on Wan 1.3B T2V [87] with 3D-RoPE, training-time KV-cache extent Ltrain=6L_{\mathrm{train}}{}=6 AR chunks (F=3F{=}3 latent frames per chunk), and a local attention window of 22 chunks, \ieΔ​ttrain+1=6\smash{\Delta t_{\mathrm{train}}}{+}1{=}6 latent frames. We provide additional experiments for LingBot-World [82] in App. E, an autoregressive world model built on a 14B backbone with Plücker camera conditioning. We use Ns=2/Nr=4\smash{N_{s}}{=}2/\smash{N_{r}}{=}4 for coherence (Sec. 4.2) and Ns=4/Nr=2\smash{N_{s}}{=}4/\smash{N_{r}}{=}2 for episodic recall (Sec. 4.3) (latent-frame slots, with Ns+Nr=Lattn=6\smash{N_{s}}+\smash{N_{r}}=\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}}{=}6).

Metrics.

Our evaluation focuses on two key aspects relevant to world models: the temporal coherence of generated outputs and the ability to correctly recall revisited locations. We evaluate coherence with TempSSIM\mathrm{TempSSIM} (↑\uparrow, SSIM [91] between consecutive decoded frames) and Local Scene Drift (↓\downarrow, mean per-chunk CLIP feature distance to the preceding chunk). For recall, we use Position-Aligned CLIP (PAC\mathrm{PAC} ↑\uparrow, CLIP-ViT-H/14 [70] cosine similarity between geometrically paired return- and forward-leg frames in loops).

Baselines.

We compare against MG2’s default sliding-window cache throughout, which evicts the oldest tokens first-in-first-out with no position correction or content compression, plus controlled variants that isolate position assignment (Block-relative, Centroid-linear, WorldTrace) and content compression (naive vs. canonical averaging, Sec. 4.2, Sec. 4.4). Episodic recall compares three retention tiers (compression, canonical-K anchoring via Latent re-anchor, and verbatim landmarks) on LoopBench and in the PAC\mathrm{PAC} sweep (Tab. 3, Tab. 10 in App. E.3). MemRoPE [42], YaRN [67], and Landmark++Block-relative are evaluated in App. E.2.

Benchmark.

We introduce LoopBench, a memory benchmark for scene revisits in AR world models. The model traces waypoints before returning to a previously visited location, and the regenerated return frame is scored against the original scene appearance at geometrically matched positions, requiring no external reference. LoopBench varies four properties of the path: waypoint count (KK, Fig. 3), rollout length (NN), camera orientation, and multi-revisit depth (RR). The full benchmark gallery with all evaluated configurations is in Fig. 8 (App. F).

4.2 Coherence: WorldTrace-Field

Virtual Position Assignment. WorldTrace-Field averages keys in the canonical domain, then assigns each averaged slot a virtual position, maintaining scene coherence under compression. We compare it against canonical-K averaging variants that apply this same key averaging but differ in position assignments. Block-relative [107] clamps offsets beyond the training horizon, so distinct older slots collapse onto a single capped position, whereas Centroid-linear positions each slot by the average timestamp of the frames it summarizes, linearly mapped into [tminv,tmaxv][\smash{t_{\min}^{v}},\smash{t_{\max}^{v}}], so slots stay distinct but their positions shift as the rollout grows. Relative to the four position properties of Sec. 3.1, Centroid-linear satisfies (i) linearity and (ii) in-distribution placement but violates (iii) horizon-stability, since its virtual positions depend on NN. Instead, our WorldTrace-Field assigns positions from slot rank alone, so every summary slot stays in-distribution and individually addressable no matter how long the rollout runs.

With the same compression approach but different position assignment shows that compression helps only when the summary slots remain addressable. With Block-relative positions, offsets beyond the training window receive zero softmax weight under local attention mask, so canonical averaging reduces to a plain sliding-window cache. Centroid-linear avoids this saturation by keeping positions within the attention mask, but its NN-dependent assignment shifts old summaries into positional ranges the model was not trained to use as the horizon grows. Our WorldTrace instead assigns positions by slot rank alone and keeps summary slots in-distribution at all horizons, outperforming Block-relative by +5.9%+5.9\% and +2.8%+2.8\% TempSSIM\mathrm{TempSSIM} and Centroid-linear by +9.5%+9.5\% and +13.8%+13.8\% at N=8N{=}8 and N=16N{=}16 (Tab. 1).

We show this qualitatively in Fig. 4, where by n=18n{=}18 the baselines drift from the initial scene context and generate incoherent geometry, while our WorldTrace-Field stays coherent. We quantify it at two horizons (N=32,48N{=}32,48) in Tab. 2, under the same canonical averaging setting. At N=32N{=}32, WorldTrace-Field achieves higher TempSSIM\mathrm{TempSSIM} (0.6130.613 vs. 0.5710.571), whereas Centroid-linear reaches the lowest Drift but at 0.040.04 lower TempSSIM\mathrm{TempSSIM}. At N=48N{=}48, WorldTrace-Field is best on both dimensions (+15.5%+15.5\% relative gain on TempSSIM\mathrm{TempSSIM}, lowest Drift), while a position assignment that depends on NN (Centroid-linear at 0.4790.479) ranks inconsistently across horizons, as its slot indices shift out-of-distribution once NN exceeds the training window. These results show that horizon-independent position assignment is the bottleneck for long-horizon generation.

4.3 Episodic Recall: WorldTrace-Landmark

While Sec. 4.2 evaluates WorldTrace-Field on open-ended rollouts, episodic recall asks whether the cache can restore a specific past scene at revisit points. We therefore test WorldTrace-Landmark (Sec. 3.4) on LoopBench (Fig. 3, Sec. 4.1) and score each return frame against scene A at matched poses with PAC\mathrm{PAC}. We show the qualitative results in Fig. 5, where the sliding-window baseline fails to reconstruct scene A at revisits, whereas WorldTrace-Landmark matches it across all three geometries.

We evaluate WorldTrace-Landmark across four difficulty tiers in Tab. 3: topology (ABA, ABCA, ABCDA), rollout length (ABA at N∈{8,16,32}N{\in}\{8,16,32\}), camera-orientation (pan 90∘90^{\circ}/180∘180^{\circ}/360∘360^{\circ} with the agent staying at A), and multi-revisit (ABABA, ABCBA, ABCDBA). All runs use Ns=4\smash{N_{s}}{=}4, Nr=2\smash{N_{r}}{=}2.

Across tiers, WorldTrace-Landmark improves PAC\mathrm{PAC} over the sliding-window baseline in every reported condition, with the largest relative gains when the KV gap to scene A is longest (Tier 2) and when multiple waypoints separate departure and return (Tier 1). Tier 3 is the hardest setting, where gains shrink at a full 360∘360^{\circ} pan, and Tier 4 shows a narrower margin on palindrome returns that revisit waypoint B before scene A. At extended horizons, we report the PAC\mathrm{PAC} sweep in Tab. 10 (App. E.3), where only verbatim landmark recall sustains PAC≈0.99\mathrm{PAC}{\approx}0.99 at N=256N{=}256, against 0.6100.610 for canonical-K anchoring. We provide further comparisons with MemRoPE and YaRN, history-selection ablations, and slot-count sensitivity in App. E.

4.4 Ablation

We isolate two design axes. (1) Position assignment (WorldTrace vs. Block-relative vs. Centroid-linear), where holding the content operator fixed and varying only positions isolates whether position, not content, is the binding constraint for WorldTrace-Field. (2) Canonical vs. naive key compression, where canonical-domain averaging avoids phase cancellation (Sec. 2.2). Its benefit surfaces on coherence (TempSSIM, LatentDiff) rather than recall. We use the ABA recall protocol with a fixed cache budget.

(1) Slot-rank positions keep summary slots addressable (Tab. 4). Naive averaging in RoPE-rotated space scores marginally higher on PAC\mathrm{PAC} at N=16N{=}16 (0.5700.570 vs. 0.5400.540), but under the same Block-relative positions it cannot reflect addressable recall, and both stay in the compression tier (≈0.4{\approx}0.4 to 0.60.6 PAC\mathrm{PAC}) far below anchoring or verbatim recall (≈0.95{\approx}0.95+, Tab. 10). Only WorldTrace keeps every summary slot in-distribution, and WorldTrace-Field accordingly recovers PAC=0.555\mathrm{PAC}{=}0.555 against 0.5400.540 for the sliding-window baseline (+0.015+0.015), a margin that grows to +0.030+0.030 at N=64N{=}64, while achieving the best TempSSIM\mathrm{TempSSIM} (0.99480.9948 vs. 0.99450.9945).

(2) Canonical key averaging avoids phase cancellation and improves coherence (Tab. 5). Holding positions fixed at Block-relative, switching from naive to canonical averaging reduces LatentDiff from 0.3120.312 to 0.2330.233 at Ns=4\smash{N_{s}}{=}4 (−25.3%-25.3\%). Under naive averaging, LatentDiff grows with Ns\smash{N_{s}} (from 0.2570.257 at Ns=1\smash{N_{s}}{=}1 to 0.3120.312 at Ns=4\smash{N_{s}}{=}4) as each additional summary slot mixes keys from frames at more diverse timestamps amplifying RoPE phase cancellation, while canonical averaging is unaffected (0.2240.224 to 0.2570.257). Averaging in canonical (unrotated) space is therefore necessary to preserve the low-frequency content of compressed summary Keys.

5 Conclusion

Long-horizon failure in autoregressive video world models is not only a matter of retaining more past content, but of keeping that content addressable. We show that temporal RoPE extrapolation can make compressed memories effectively unreadable once rollouts move beyond the training horizon, and introduce WorldTrace, a training-free cache mechanism that keeps distant traces at fixed in-distribution virtual positions. Within this addressable cache, WorldTrace-Field provides a coherence-oriented summary of history, while WorldTrace-Landmark preserves verbatim traces for episodic recall. Empirically, WorldTrace-Field improves Temporal Consistency by +15.5% at N=48N=48, and WorldTrace-Landmark raises Scene Consistency by +19.5% on LoopBench ABA loops, extending visually persistent generation from seconds toward minute-scale return-to-origin rollouts.

More broadly, WorldTrace suggests that memory for video world models should be designed around two questions: how to ensure past content remains addressable, and what kind of visual traces should be stored for future queries. The two variants studied here represent different points in this design space, with smooth summaries supporting temporal coherence and sparse landmarks supporting recall of specific places. This perspective also clarifies the limits of the current method. WorldTrace is designed for temporal-RoPE autoregressive models with a fixed KV-cache budget, and its current content writers instantiate only two simple structured projections of history, so that WorldTrace-Field favors coherence but can blur specific scene details, while WorldTrace-Landmark preserves specific places but depends on detecting and retaining the right scene entries. Future memory systems may need to choose these projections more adaptively, especially important in interactive settings where agents move freely, revisit locations, and query the past from changing viewpoints. In this view, WorldTrace-Field and WorldTrace-Landmark are not endpoints, but two structured approximations to the same underlying problem of projecting a long visual history into a small addressable cache.
