Appendix A Notation

Appendix B WorldTrace as Structured Sparse Attention

Under autoregressive decoding with full attention over the history, each new chunk attends to all TT past frames, so both the per-step attention cost and the KV cache grow as O⁡(T)O\!\left(T\right) with generation length. Video world models typically cap this with a fixed-size sliding window over the most recent frames. Our WorldTrace instead introduces structured sparse approximations that aim to compress the full TT-frame history to Lattn≪T\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}}\ll T effective tokens via a projection matrix P∈ℝLattn×TP\in\mathbb{R}^{\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}}\times T}, where each row defines which frames contribute to one compressed slot. Throughout this section, KK denotes the canonical (unrotated) key matrix, which is the domain in which the canonical-store operator applies PP. The slot-rank re-encoding of Def. 1 is applied afterwards at attention time, which is the same fixed, in-distribution rotation on the compressed cache.

B.1 Full and Projected Attention

For a single query qq, the standard attention output is 𝒜⁡(q,K,V)=softmax⁡(q​K⊤)​V=αq​V\mathcal{A}(q,K,V)=\operatorname{softmax}(q\,K^{\top})\,V=\smash{\alpha_{q}}\,V, a weighted sum over all TT value vectors with αq∈ΔT\smash{\alpha_{q}}\in\Delta_{T}, where ΔT\Delta_{T} is the probability simplex over the TT past frames (non-negative weights summing to one). The projected attention approximation replaces the TT-token sequence with Lattn≪T\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}}\ll T prototype tokens (one per compressed slot) defined by a row-stochastic matrix P∈ℝLattn×TP\in\mathbb{R}^{\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}}\times T}, meaning each row of PP is itself a distribution over past frames (this property is what makes the bounds of Sec. B.3 non-vacuous):

𝒜^​(q,K,V,P)=softmax⁡(q​(P​K)⊤)​P​V,\widehat{\mathcal{A}}(q,K,V;\,P)\;=\;\operatorname{softmax}(q\,(PK)^{\top})\,PV, (5)

where α^q=softmax⁡(q​(P​K)⊤)∈ΔLattn\smash{\hat{\alpha}_{q}}=\operatorname{softmax}(q\,(PK)^{\top})\in\Delta_{\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}}} are the prototype attention weights, now a distribution over the Lattn\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}} compressed slots rather than the TT frames, and Pi​VP_{i}V is the compressed value for slot ii.

Relation to prior structured-attention approximations.

Eq. (5) is the low-rank factorization of attention studied by efficient transformer architectures, whose projections are learned or trained end-to-end [89, 102, 86, 6, 85, 45]. WorldTrace differs mainly in that the projection is applied training-free at inference time to a pretrained model’s KV cache. Beyond this, two design choices follow from the RoPE-based world-model setting rather than marking a contrast with these methods. First, PP acts in the canonical key domain, so merging avoids the phase cancellation (Sec. 2.2). Second, the compressed slots are re-encoded at slot-rank virtual positions (Def. 1), keeping them addressable beyond the training horizon. The row structure of PP (uniform averaging for WorldTrace-Field, one-hot selection for WorldTrace-Landmark) then determines whether compression favors coherence or recall, as formalized below.

B.2 Structured Attention Approximations Unified by PP

The four cache structures (Fig. 6) compared in our experiments correspond to four structured choices of PP.

Sliding window attention.

Here P=[ 0​ILattn]P=[\,0\;\;I_{\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}}}\,] makes each row a one-hot vector selecting one of the most recent Lattn\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}} frames, discarding all earlier history (Fig. 6a). Adding an attention sink anchor is a simple modification (Fig. 6b) in which row 0 is pinned to the first (sink) frame while the remaining Lattn−1\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}}{-}1 rows select the most recent Lattn−1\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}}{-}1 frames verbatim, always keeping a global context token in cache regardless of generation length. This anchor mitigates the collapse of the attention distribution onto only local tokens at long generation horizons [98].

WorldTrace-Field.

Rows corresponding to the Nr\smash{N_{r}} recent slots are identity rows as above. Each remaining row is a uniform average over the MM frames assigned to its summary slot (Fig. 6c), setting Pi,t=1/MP_{i,t}=1/M if frame tt is assigned to slot ii and 00 otherwise.

WorldTrace-Landmark.

Summary rows are one-hot selectors at the detected scene-entry frames (Fig. 6d), so the row storing the landmark at timestamp tℓ∗\smash{t_{\ell^{*}}} has Pi,t=1P_{i,t}=1 for t=tℓ∗t=\smash{t_{\ell^{*}}} and 00 otherwise, simply copying that stored key, Pi​K=K⁡[tℓ∗]P_{i}K=K[\smash{t_{\ell^{*}}}], matching the frozen key of Eq. (4). The rows update as generation proceeds, with a new scene-entry frame overwriting a summary row and, once all rows are full, the oldest landmark evicted to make room for the newest. These choices span a spectrum of PP-row structures, from sparse (one-hot selection) to dense (uniform averaging).

B.3 Approximation Quality and Error Decomposition

The cache contents, and hence PP, change as generation proceeds, since the recent window slides and summary rows are filled or overwritten. All statements in this and the following subsections therefore refer to one generation step at a time, where TT and PP denote the history length and the projection realized by the cache at the current step, and 𝒬\mathcal{Q} denotes the queries of the chunk being generated (one attention row per query token and head). Every bound holds at each step separately, and no single static PP is claimed to serve all steps.

Two sources of error.

The compressed cache differs from an unbounded cache in two independent ways: keys are repositioned (re-encoded at slot-rank virtual positions rather than their original timestamps), and keys are compressed (merged through PP). Writing 𝒜orig\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{orig}} for full attention with keys at their original positions, 𝒜\mathcal{A} for full attention with keys re-encoded at virtual positions, and 𝒜^\widehat{\mathcal{A}} for the projected attention of Eq. (5) on the re-encoded cache, the total error decomposes as:

‖𝒜^−𝒜orig‖≤‖𝒜−𝒜orig‖⏟repositioning+‖𝒜^−𝒜‖⏟compression.\|\widehat{\mathcal{A}}-\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{orig}}\|\;\leq\;\underbrace{\|\mathcal{A}-\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{orig}}\|}_{\text{repositioning}}\;+\;\underbrace{\|\widehat{\mathcal{A}}-\mathcal{A}\|}_{\text{compression}}.

The repositioning term is not an artifact of compression but the trade-off for addressability. Beyond the training horizon the original offsets are out-of-distribution and attention degrades outright (Sec. 2.1), so slot-rank re-encoding trades an uncontrolled OOD failure for a bounded, in-distribution position shift. We do not bound this term analytically, but it is measured empirically by the position ablation (Tab. 1), which varies only the position assignment with the writer held fixed. Prop. 1 below bounds the compression term. All statements in this section are relative to the repositioned reference 𝒜\mathcal{A}.

For a single query qq, let α^q=softmax⁡(q​(P​K)⊤)∈ΔLattn\smash{\hat{\alpha}_{q}}=\operatorname{softmax}(q\,(PK)^{\top})\in\Delta_{\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}}} be the prototype attention weights under the compressed cache, and define the output error rq​(P)=𝒜^​(q,K,V,P)−𝒜⁡(q,K,V)\smash{r_{q}(P)}=\widehat{\mathcal{A}}(q,K,V;\,P)-\mathcal{A}(q,K,V).

Proposition 1 (Approximation bound).
‖rq​(P)‖2≤‖α^q​P−αq‖1⏟distribution mismatch⋅‖V‖∞,row,\|\smash{r_{q}(P)}\|_{2}\;\leq\;\underbrace{\|\smash{\hat{\alpha}_{q}}P-\smash{\alpha_{q}}\|_{1}}_{\text{distribution mismatch}}\;\cdot\;\|V\|_{\infty,\mathrm{row}},

where ‖V‖∞,row=maxt⁡‖V⁡[t]‖2\|V\|_{\infty,\mathrm{row}}=\max_{t}\|V[t]\|_{2}.

Proof.

By associativity 𝒜^=α^q​(P​V)=(α^q​P)​V\widehat{\mathcal{A}}=\smash{\hat{\alpha}_{q}}(PV)=(\smash{\hat{\alpha}_{q}}P)V, so rq​(P)=(α^q​P−αq)​V=∑tct​V​[t]\smash{r_{q}(P)}=(\smash{\hat{\alpha}_{q}}P-\smash{\alpha_{q}})V=\sum_{t}c_{t}\,V[t] with c=α^q​P−αqc=\smash{\hat{\alpha}_{q}}P-\smash{\alpha_{q}}. The vector-valued Hölder inequality (ℓ1\ell_{1}/ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} duality) on the rows of VV then gives ‖rq​(P)‖2≤‖c‖1​‖V‖∞,row\|\smash{r_{q}(P)}\|_{2}\leq\|c\|_{1}\,\|V\|_{\infty,\mathrm{row}}. ∎

The bound motivates minimizing distribution mismatch ‖α^q​P−αq‖1\|\smash{\hat{\alpha}_{q}}P-\smash{\alpha_{q}}\|_{1} independently of value geometry. For WorldTrace-Field, Prop. 2 (stated later in App. C) ensures the compressed key Kfieldf​(tv){K}_{\mathrm{field}}^{f}\!\left(t^{v}\right) reproduces the mean attention score of its source keys at the shared virtual position, limiting per-slot mismatch when query preferences vary smoothly across a group. For WorldTrace-Landmark, a verbatim scene-entry key keeps the mismatch small for queries concentrated on that event, the recall condition of Eq. (8) in Sec. B.5.

B.4 Reduction to Nonnegative Matrix Factorization

Nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF) approximates a nonnegative matrix as the product of two low-rank nonnegative factors [44], which form a compact summary of the original data. Compressing attention through PP is an instance of this problem. Treat α^q∈ΔLattn\smash{\hat{\alpha}_{q}}\in\Delta_{\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}}} as a free variable (decoupling it from the softmax in Eq. (5)), and define 𝐀∈ℝ|𝒬|×T\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{Q}|\times T} as the matrix whose rows are the full attention distributions αq\smash{\alpha_{q}}, one row per query in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, and 𝐁∈ℝ|𝒬|×Lattn\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{Q}|\times\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}}} as the matrix whose rows are the corresponding prototype weights α^q\smash{\hat{\alpha}_{q}}. The aggregate distribution-mismatch objective then becomes:

min𝐁≥0,P≥0⁡‖𝐁​P−𝐀‖1subject to row-sum constraints on ​𝐁​ and ​P,\min_{\mathbf{B}\geq 0,\;P\geq 0}\|\mathbf{B}P-\mathbf{A}\|_{1}\quad\text{subject to row-sum constraints on }\mathbf{B}\text{ and }P,

which is NMF with an ℓ1\ell_{1} fidelity term, in the spirit of robust NMF formulations [43]. This relaxation serves the analysis only, because at inference α^q\smash{\hat{\alpha}_{q}} is not free but determined by PP through the softmax, α^q=softmax⁡(q​(P​K)⊤)\smash{\hat{\alpha}_{q}}=\operatorname{softmax}(q\,(PK)^{\top}) for each query qq and key matrix KK, and Sec. B.5 accounts for the gap through the lower-bound relation.

Each structural constraint on PP then recovers a WorldTrace variant and a known clustering algorithm, spanning the sparse-to-dense spectrum. The uniform-partition rows of WorldTrace-Field are a fixed-assignment, ℓ1\ell_{1} (total-variation) analog of kk-means with cluster-mean prototypes, with the time-ordered partition replacing the learned assignment step. The 0/1 rows of WorldTrace-Landmark, with α^q\smash{\hat{\alpha}_{q}} constrained to hard assignment, reduce to kk-medoids on attention distributions, for which the canonical-key cosine-distance rule is a lightweight single-pass O⁡(1)O\!\left(1\right)-per-chunk surrogate.

B.5 When Are WorldTrace Projections Close to Optimal?

The NMF objective above is deliberately broad, since without assumptions on the query distribution no fixed Lattn\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}}-row projection can be uniformly optimal. Any reachable compressed distribution has the form γ​P\gamma P, where the slot-weight vector γ∈ΔLattn\gamma\in\Delta_{\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}}} mixes the Lattn\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}} rows of PP. Since each row is a distribution over the TT frames, the Lattn\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}} rows together place total weight Lattn\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}} across the TT columns. Averaged over the columns, some frame tt therefore receives at most maxi⁡Pi,t≤Lattn/T\max_{i}P_{i,t}\leq\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}}/T, so a query concentrating on that one frame has mismatch ‖γ​P−𝐞t‖1=2​(1−(γ​P)t)≥2​(1−Lattn/T)\|\gamma P-\mathbf{e}_{t}\|_{1}=2\bigl(1-(\gamma P)_{t}\bigr)\geq 2(1-\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}}/T) for every γ\gamma. Intuitively, the compressed cache can place at most an Lattn/T\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}}/T fraction of its attention on any single frame, so it cannot reproduce a query that focuses on one frame, and the error grows as the compression ratio Lattn/T\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}}/T shrinks. A compressed cache therefore needs to choose which parts of history to preserve. We define one target query family per variant, a definition rather than an assumption about the pretrained model, and show each variant near-optimal on its own family under the following relaxed mismatch objective, the total ℓ1\ell_{1} gap between each query’s true attention αq\smash{\alpha_{q}} and the closest distribution reachable from the Lattn\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}} compressed slots:

𝒥⁡(P)=∑q∈𝒬minγq∈ΔLattn⁡‖γq​P−αq‖1.\mathcal{J}(P)=\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}}\min_{\gamma_{q}\in\Delta_{\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}}}}\|\gamma_{q}P-\smash{\alpha_{q}}\|_{1}.

Here γq\gamma_{q} is chosen freely per query. At inference the slot weights are instead fixed by the softmax, α^q=softmax⁡(q​(P​K)⊤)\smash{\hat{\alpha}_{q}}=\operatorname{softmax}(q\,(PK)^{\top}), so 𝒥⁡(P)\mathcal{J}(P) is a lower bound on the true inference objective, and the bounds we derive are for this relaxed version.

Recent-window mass.

Split the attention as αq=(αqold,αqrec)\smash{\alpha_{q}}=(\smash{\alpha_{q}}^{\mathrm{old}},\smash{\alpha_{q}}^{\mathrm{rec}}), the weights on old and on recent frames. Both projections keep the Nr\smash{N_{r}} most recent frames as identity rows, which reproduce αqrec\smash{\alpha_{q}}^{\mathrm{rec}} exactly, so compression error arises only on old history. The conditions below therefore involve only the old-history attention, normalized to the distribution α¯qold=αqold/‖αqold‖1\smash{\bar{\alpha}_{q}^{\mathrm{old}}}=\smash{\alpha_{q}}^{\mathrm{old}}/\|\smash{\alpha_{q}}^{\mathrm{old}}\|_{1}.

Coherent queries: group-level attention.

Partition the old history into Ns\smash{N_{s}} contiguous temporal groups, one per summary slot, and let uiu_{i} be the uniform distribution over the frames in group ii. Call a query qq εq\varepsilon_{q}-coherent if its old-history attention depends on groups rather than individual frames, meaning there exists a distribution aq∈ΔNsa_{q}\in\Delta_{\smash{N_{s}}} such that:

‖α¯qold−∑iaq,i​ui‖1≤εq,\Bigl\|\smash{\bar{\alpha}_{q}^{\mathrm{old}}}-\sum_{i}a_{q,i}u_{i}\Bigr\|_{1}\leq\varepsilon_{q}, (6)

which is the coherence condition. For a query set 𝒬\mathcal{Q} of εq\varepsilon_{q}-coherent queries, the WorldTrace-Field projection PfieldP_{\mathrm{field}} satisfies:

𝒥⁡(Pfield)≤∑q∈𝒬‖αqold‖1​εq≤∑q∈𝒬εq.\mathcal{J}(P_{\mathrm{field}})\leq\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}}\|\smash{\alpha_{q}}^{\mathrm{old}}\|_{1}\,\varepsilon_{q}\leq\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}}\varepsilon_{q}. (7)

Choosing γq=(‖αqold‖1​aq,αqrec)\gamma_{q}=\bigl(\|\smash{\alpha_{q}}^{\mathrm{old}}\|_{1}\,a_{q},\;\smash{\alpha_{q}}^{\mathrm{rec}}\bigr) copies αqrec\smash{\alpha_{q}}^{\mathrm{rec}} exactly and leaves old-history error at most ‖αqold‖1​εq\|\smash{\alpha_{q}}^{\mathrm{old}}\|_{1}\,\varepsilon_{q}. Since 𝒥⁡(P)≥0\mathcal{J}(P)\geq 0 for any projection, WorldTrace-Field is within ∑qεq\sum_{q}\varepsilon_{q} of the best possible projection for this query family. The canonical averaging produces these uniform rows in a RoPE-invariant domain, keeping each group mean addressable at its virtual position.

Recall queries: sparse scene-entry attention.

For episodic recall, a return query wants one specific past scene rather than a smooth summary. At most Ns\smash{N_{s}} landmarks are stored. Call a query qq δq\delta_{q}-covered if the landmark frame it targets, written m⁡(q)m(q), satisfies:

‖α¯qold−𝐞m⁡(q)‖1≤δq,\|\smash{\bar{\alpha}_{q}^{\mathrm{old}}}-\mathbf{e}_{m(q)}\|_{1}\leq\delta_{q}, (8)

where 𝐞m⁡(q)\mathbf{e}_{m(q)} is the one-hot distribution on that frame. Eqn. (8) is the recall condition. For a query set 𝒬\mathcal{Q} of δq\delta_{q}-covered queries, the WorldTrace-Landmark projection PlandmarkP_{\mathrm{landmark}} satisfies:

𝒥⁡(Plandmark)≤∑q∈𝒬‖αqold‖1​δq≤∑q∈𝒬δq.\mathcal{J}(P_{\mathrm{landmark}})\leq\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}}\|\smash{\alpha_{q}}^{\mathrm{old}}\|_{1}\,\delta_{q}\leq\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}}\delta_{q}. (9)

The construction is the same with 𝐞s⁡(q)\mathbf{e}_{s(q)} in place of aqa_{q}, where s⁡(q)s(q) is the landmark slot whose row copies frame m⁡(q)m(q), so WorldTrace-Landmark is close to the best one-hot projection whenever the detector forms a δ\delta-cover of the recall targets. The oldest-out scene-entry rule of our experiments is a streaming approximation to this cover, reliable when at most Ns\smash{N_{s}} scenes are simultaneously relevant.

What these bounds do and do not claim.

Eq. (7) and Eq. (9) are conditional characterizations, true by construction for the query families that Eq. (6) and Eq. (8) define, not unconditional optimality claims. We do not measure εq\varepsilon_{q} or δq\delta_{q} on the pretrained model, since that would require uncompressed rollouts past the training horizon, where Sec. 2.1 shows the reference attention itself degrades. Each condition is instead tested through the behavior it predicts.

Future directions.

The NMF framing points to several natural extensions, including online kk-means or streaming coresets [22] that adapt partition boundaries at inference time, soft-sparse rows that interpolate between averaging and verbatim selection, and a directly optimized PP that balances coherence and recall across all queries in a rollout.

Appendix C Additional Properties

Temporal RoPE at long horizons.

We provide temporal-RoPE background for the addressability failure in Sec. 2.1 and expand Eq. (3), summarized at the end of Sec. 3.3. We analyze which temporal RoPE frequencies stay in-distribution at long horizons in MG2-1.3B, and which reach rotation angles the model never saw in training, making their contribution to the attention score effectively random. MG2-1.3B inherits the 3D RoPE split of the Wan 2.1 backbone [87]. The 128-dimensional per-head embedding is divided across three position axes: 2​ct=442\smash{c_{t}}{=}44 dimensions for temporal position and 2​ch=2​cw=422\smash{c_{h}}{=}2\smash{c_{w}}{=}42 dimensions each for spatial height and width, with shared base θ=10000\theta=10000. The ff-th temporal frequency is θf=θ−f/ct\smash{\theta_{f}}=\theta^{-f/\smash{c_{t}}} for f=0,…,ct−1f=0,\ldots,\smash{c_{t}}{-}1, ranging from θf=1.0\smash{\theta_{f}}{=}1.0 at f=0f{=}0 (fastest rotating) down to θf≈1.5×10−4\smash{\theta_{f}}\approx 1.5\times 10^{-4} (slowest).

Frequency ff enters the attention score through cos⁡(θf​|δq,k|)\cos(\smash{\theta_{f}}|\smash{\delta_{q,k}}|), where δq,k=q−k\smash{\delta_{q,k}}=q-k is the query-key offset. When θf​|δq,k|≪π\smash{\theta_{f}}|\smash{\delta_{q,k}}|\ll\pi, the cosine stays near 11, and the component is position-invariant and carries semantic content. When θf​|δq,k|≫π\smash{\theta_{f}}|\smash{\delta_{q,k}}|\gg\pi, the phase wraps past π\pi many times, so the cosine takes an essentially arbitrary value at each offset and the component stops signaling how far away the key is. The consequence is instability in the fastest components, where moving a key by a single offset step shifts the phase by up to 11 rad, so the contribution these components make to the score can change substantially, even in sign, between neighboring offsets, and recall degrades steadily over a long rollout. This wavelength-vs-context view follows YaRN’s NTK-by-parts framing [67], which likewise groups RoPE dimensions by how their wavelength compares to the context length and treats the short-wavelength (fast) and long-wavelength (slow) groups differently.

Concretely, at the training max offset Δ​ttrain=5\smash{\Delta t_{\mathrm{train}}}=5, components f≥10f\geq 10 satisfy θf×5<0.08\smash{\theta_{f}}\times 5<0.08 rad and act as near-semantic carriers. At a representative long-horizon offset |δq,k|=30|\smash{\delta_{q,k}}|=30, the three fastest components (f≤2f\leq 2) all exceed 3​π3\pi rad, with f=3f{=}3 at 8.5 rad and f=5f{=}5 at 3.7 rad. We show the phase θf​|δq,k|\smash{\theta_{f}}|\smash{\delta_{q,k}}| across all frequencies and inference distances in Fig. 7, over a plotted distance range chosen for illustration only, since in an unbounded rollout the offset grows past it and pushes ever more components beyond π\pi. The long-horizon failure is therefore driven by the fast components alone, while the slow components remain reliable semantic carriers even at large offsets. This motivates the position-side intervention of WorldTrace, which places every compressed slot at an in-distribution virtual offset and thereby keeps the fast components within their trained phase range at any horizon.

Mean attention preservation.

The WorldTrace-Field compression preserves the mean attention score, so that a single summary token Kfieldf​(tv){K}_{\mathrm{field}}^{f}\!\left(t^{v}\right) reproduces exactly the average of the scores its MM source keys would produce if all were relocated to the shared virtual position tvt^{v}, for every query and every temporal RoPE frequency. This matters because attention scores are the only channel through which the model reads the cache, so compression that silently changed them would bias the model toward or away from distant history, precisely the failure the pretrained attention never learned to correct.

Proposition 2 (Mean attention preservation).

Fix a temporal RoPE pair ff and a virtual position tvt^{v}. For any query Qqf\smash{Q_{q}^{f}},

⟨Qqf,Kfieldf​(tv)⟩=1M​∑m=1M⟨Qqf,R⁡(θf​tv)​Kmf⟩.\bigl\langle\smash{Q_{q}^{f}},{K}_{\mathrm{field}}^{f}\!\left(t^{v}\right)\bigr\rangle=\frac{1}{M}\sum\nolimits_{m=1}^{M}\bigl\langle\smash{Q_{q}^{f}},R\!\left(\smash{\theta_{f}}t^{v}\right)\smash{K_{m}^{f}}\bigr\rangle.
Proof.

By Eq. (3), Kfieldf​(tv)=R⁡(θf​tv)​K¯f{K}_{\mathrm{field}}^{f}\!\left(t^{v}\right)=R\!\left(\smash{\theta_{f}}t^{v}\right)\smash{\bar{K}^{f}} with K¯f=1M​∑m=1MKmf\smash{\bar{K}^{f}}=\tfrac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\smash{K_{m}^{f}}. Since the rotation R⁡(θf​tv)R\!\left(\smash{\theta_{f}}t^{v}\right) is linear and the inner product is linear in its second argument,

⟨Qqf,Kfieldf​(tv)⟩=⟨Qqf,R⁡(θf​tv)​(1M​∑m=1MKmf)⟩=1M​∑m=1M⟨Qqf,R⁡(θf​tv)​Kmf⟩.\bigl\langle\smash{Q_{q}^{f}},{K}_{\mathrm{field}}^{f}\!\left(t^{v}\right)\bigr\rangle=\Bigl\langle\smash{Q_{q}^{f}},\,R\!\left(\smash{\theta_{f}}t^{v}\right)\Bigl(\frac{1}{M}\sum\nolimits_{m=1}^{M}\smash{K_{m}^{f}}\Bigr)\Bigr\rangle=\frac{1}{M}\sum\nolimits_{m=1}^{M}\bigl\langle\smash{Q_{q}^{f}},R\!\left(\smash{\theta_{f}}t^{v}\right)\smash{K_{m}^{f}}\bigr\rangle.

∎

Consequently, the compressed representation separates content from position by design, storing only the canonical content average K¯f\smash{\bar{K}^{f}} in a slot whose temporal identity comes entirely from its virtual position tvt^{v}. This separation is exactly what slot-rank addressing needs, because the stored content carries no leftover phase from its source timestamps, letting WorldTrace place a slot at any virtual position (Def. 1) where a query reads the same content. Prop. 2 also pins down this design by showing that any linear operator preserving the mean attention score for every query must output the same canonical average K¯f\smash{\bar{K}^{f}}, leaving only the virtual position tvt^{v} free, which WorldTrace sets by slot rank (Sec. 3.1). Constraining an operator through the structure of the RoPE rotation it inverts has antecedents in structured-Jacobian parameterizations [57]. One side effect of averaging is a norm reduction, since mutually uncorrelated canonical keys average to roughly 1/M1/\sqrt{M} times the norm of a single key, so a summary slot enters the softmax with a smaller logit than a verbatim key. We keep this behavior rather than restoring the norm with a M\sqrt{M} rescale, both because the smaller logit softly downweights heavily compressed history relative to the verbatim recent window and because the rescale did not help at long horizons.

Appendix D Related Work

D.1 Memory-Augmented Transformers

Memory-augmented transformers pair a recent verbatim window with a compressed record of older context, realized as segment-level recurrence with relative positions [19], a compressed memory of older tokens [71], external kkNN memory [97], learned memory tokens passed between segments [7, 39], and a fused sliding window plus compressive memory [64]. WorldTrace adopts the same two-tier structure, with a recent verbatim window plus compressed summary slots. Landmark Attention [63] shares vocabulary with WorldTrace-Landmark, but its landmarks are trained representatives that gate attention to off-cache blocks at 1D position, whereas WorldTrace-Landmark is training-free, stores verbatim canonical-frame keys inside the O⁡(1)O(1) cache, and freezes them against unrotate-and-rerotate drift in 3D RoPE. The broader spectrum toward compressed state spans linear attention [40], Mamba [26], and Test-Time Training [80]. We target the fixed-budget, training-free setting in AR video world models.

D.2 KV Cache Compression for Large Language Models

LLM KV-cache methods fall into three families: window/eviction [4, 98, 115, 53, 9], merging [6, 83], and quantization [56], the last orthogonal to the position-OOD failure we target. DuoAttention [99] splits heads into retrieval and streaming families, parallel to our recent-window and summary-slot split. These methods change content only, picking which tokens to keep or merge rather than which virtual position a summary spanning several merged frames should occupy. The closest exceptions touch per-token positional structure [119, 31] or unrotate and rerotate individually retained keys [16, 65], but none reassign summary-slot positions. Our setting also differs from LLM compression in that keys accumulate across independently denoised AR video chunks, so importance must be ranked under denoising-timestep-conditioned queries. Under such queries, angular-concentration scores [61] lose the stable pre-RoPE key geometry they assume, and layer-budget reallocations [9, 114] tune which layers keep tokens rather than how summary slots are addressed at read time. WorldTrace-Field instead averages canonical keys and pairs the result with slot-rank positions.

D.3 Position Extrapolation for RoPE

RoPE [78] degrades past trained relative offsets. Existing fixes span index rescaling [13, 67, 74], alternative distance biases [69, 81], position-free training [41], and frequency- or content-aware encodings [24, 36], while vision and video extensions add 2D/3D splits [34, 93], camera-relative encodings [50], and training-free diffusion extrapolation [116]. All of this remaps positions for individually retained tokens or fixed-length inputs. Our cache instead needs to be compressed, since a fixed O⁡(1)O(1) budget cannot keep every past frame verbatim. Each merged summary then needs an explicit virtual position, a quantity that does not arise when tokens keep separate identities, and WorldTrace assigns slot-rank offsets for that role without retraining. Wang et al. [88] tie position to numerical precision, consistent with our coupling thesis (Sec. 3.5). UCM [104] and MosaicMem [111] warp 3D positions for camera-controlled worlds as geometry-driven, trained operators.

D.4 Autoregressive Video World Models

Interactive AR video world models [25, 32, 20, 84] generate via chunk-wise diffusion prediction, dominantly under the Self-Forcing paradigm [38, 10, 75, 109], which aligns training rollouts with the model’s own KV cache and inherits a local attention window not sized for arbitrarily long inference. Training-time horizon extensions [18, 37] are covered with memory-specific methods in Sec. D.5. Foundation backbones [87] and the world-model lineage from Ha and Schmidhuber [29] through Dreamer [30] to closed-loop driving simulators [3] motivate interactive rollouts beyond passive long-form generation.

D.5 Memory and KV Cache for Video World Models

Inference-time KV cache.

Closest to WorldTrace, inference-time methods modify cache read/write without retraining. Position-side fixes remap or cap temporal offsets via block-relative RoPE with aggressive flushing [107], inference-time position adjustment [17, 47], or per-token virtual positions with cross-frame decay [48]. Content-side writers decide what to merge, prune, or retain, through re-aligned sink tokens [108], dual-rate EMA summaries [42], importance pruning [11, 46], and temporal-correspondence merging [73]. FlowCache [60] targets per-step compute rather than long-horizon recall, but its recent-summary structure parallels ours. These methods adjust the position side, the content side, or pair the two without designing them jointly. To our knowledge, none combines a position assignment that keeps an arbitrary number of compressed slots distinct at any horizon with summary writes performed in the canonical pre-RoPE domain. WorldTrace couples exactly these two (WorldTrace-Field compresses, WorldTrace-Landmark freezes), keeping every slot addressable inside a fixed O⁡(1)O(1) cache.

Training-time extensions.

Training-time methods finetune the generator itself for longer effective context. One line pairs partitioned caches or memory hierarchies with RoPE re-alignment or long-context teacher supervision [12, 105, 14, 49, 52, 117, 55]. Memory-decomposition approaches assign different parts of history to dedicated modules [77, 94, 8]. Architectural long-horizon models train for extended rollouts rather than patching a fixed checkpoint [27, 66, 79, 112, 120], and Sparse Forcing [103] learns block-sparse attention with persistent anchors end-to-end. Po et al. [68] extend the effective context of a video world model with a trained state-space memory and evaluate it on Memory Maze with a spatial retrieval task, where the model is given a trajectory as context and then backtracks the exact action sequence to the starting position. WorldTrace needs no retraining, restoring addressability by changing cache read/write on a fixed checkpoint.

Geometry-conditioned memory.

Trained methods decide what to keep in memory based on camera pose, actions, or scene geometry, drawing on pose- and action-annotated compressed latents [35], warped positions or latents for camera-controlled worlds [111, 104, 62], co-visibility-based selection [23], pose-tagged frame re-injection [100], and camera-aware memory gating [28]. WorldTrace is geometry-free, replacing pose-, action-, or co-visibility-driven memory selection with slot-rank positions and canonical cache writes.

External memory banks and retrieval.

Rather than compressing inside the KV cache, these systems store or retrieve frames outside it and re-inject them via auxiliary attention or re-encoding, through FOV-based frame selection [92], importance-weighted frame contexts [113], first-chunk appearance anchoring [33], cached latent banks [95, 51, 110], and global-state retrieval [15]. WorldTrace keeps memory in the KV cache under one O⁡(1)O(1) recent-plus-summary budget, with no external bank, re-encoding, or retrieval.

Comparison.

In Tab. 7, we qualitatively compare memory approaches on four axes: whether positional OOD is fixed, whether memory is bounded, whether intermediate history is preserved, and whether retraining is required. For evaluation, WorldScore [21], MIND [106], and VBench-2.0 [118] assess long-horizon quality, and Lian et al. [54] targets revisit consistency in Minecraft. The Memory Maze retrieval task of Po et al. [68] is the closest published revisit test to ours and scores a backtracked trajectory against the recorded ground-truth frames, whereas LoopBench sweeps loop topology, rollout length, camera orientation, and multi-revisit depth and scores each return against the model’s own earlier generation at matched poses, so it needs no ground-truth footage of the revisited scene.

Appendix E Additional Experimental Results

E.1 Unified Cache Allocation

Sec. 4.2 and Sec. 4.3 evaluate the two content writers separately, while a single long rollout typically asks for both coherent continuation and reliable revisits. The slot-rank cache of Def. 1 is a shared interface, so the two writers can occupy the same cache and the only decision is how to divide the fixed slot budget between them. Every summary slot that does not hold a landmark stays a WorldTrace-Field average.

We sweep the full allocation from all-WorldTrace-Field to all-WorldTrace-Landmark at the fixed budget of Ns=4\smash{N_{s}}{=}4 summary slots and report both metrics in Tab. 8. The all-landmark end of the sweep is the strongest on recall at every horizon and reaches PAC=0.866\mathrm{PAC}{=}0.866, 0.8270.827, and 0.8170.817 at N=16N{=}16, 3232, and 4848, above the sliding-window baseline in each case. The intermediate allocations do not interpolate monotonically between the two ends, and at N=32N{=}32 and N=48N{=}48 several of them sit slightly below the baseline, so on these runs the gain comes from dedicating slots to landmarks rather than from any particular mixture. The practical conclusion is that one cache serves both workloads with no retraining and no additional memory, and that the split follows from which behavior a given rollout needs rather than from tuning.

E.2 Training-Free Positional Baselines

We compare MemRoPE [42] and YaRN [67] on the Sec. 4.3 ABA loops in Tab. 9, factoring the position scheme (Block-relative vs. WorldTrace) from the content writer at two horizons.

MemRoPE [42] (Block-relative ++ dual-rate EMA with αlong=0.01\alpha_{\mathrm{long}}{=}0.01 and αshort=0.1\alpha_{\mathrm{short}}{=}0.1, matching the original release) survives OOD positions via EMA decay but is still beaten by Landmark++Block-relative, because verbatim canonical keys retain stronger query-key similarity than smoothed averages, and WorldTrace-Landmark adds in-distribution positions on top. MemRoPE++WorldTrace (Block-relative swapped for WorldTrace, EMA kept) degrades (p<0.001p{<}0.001) because its write and read offsets disagree.

YaRN [67] rescales temporal RoPE frequencies to bring offsets back in-distribution, gaining +22%+22\% over the sliding-window baseline at N=32N{=}32 (p<0.001p{<}0.001) and confirming position is the primary bottleneck. However, it needs O⁡(N)O(N) memory (OOM by ∼N=100{\sim}N{=}100), and the rescale diverges with horizon. WorldTrace-Landmark exceeds it by a wide margin at N=32N{=}32 (0.9640.964 vs. 0.4900.490) in O⁡(1)O(1) memory and stays near-constant through N=512N{=}512.

E.3 Scene Consistency Episodic Recall Sweep

We report the full PAC\mathrm{PAC} breakdown across N∈{16,32,48,64,128,256}N\in\{16,32,48,64,128,256\} on ABA loops (Ns=4\smash{N_{s}}{=}4, Nr=2\smash{N_{r}}{=}2) in Tab. 10 and partition methods by retained past content into three tiers: compression-only (sliding window, Naive, WorldTrace-Field), canonical-K anchoring (Latent re-anchor, WorldTrace-Field with scene anchoring), and verbatim recall (WorldTrace-Landmark). Within compression, WorldTrace-Field beats the sliding-window baseline at N=32N{=}32 to 6464 (p<0.001p{<}0.001, paired tt-test). Anchoring lifts recall by 4040 to 5050 points at moderate horizons. Only verbatim recall sustains it at N=256N{=}256. At N=256N{=}256 the canonical-K tier’s PAC\mathrm{PAC} falls to 0.6100.610 while WorldTrace-Landmark holds at 0.9890.989.

E.4 Cross-Architecture Experiments

In Tab. 11, we report PAC\mathrm{PAC} at 2×2{\times} to 8×8{\times} training horizon on LingBot-World [82] with WorldTrace applied. LingBot-World is a mixture-of-experts diffusion transformer built on a 14B backbone with Plücker camera conditioning, and MG2 is a dense 1.3B model without it, so this comparison varies both scale and architecture. The recall gain that WorldTrace-Landmark delivers on both backbones indicates that the positional bottleneck we identify follows the trained offset range rather than parameter count. WorldTrace-Field tracks the sliding-window baseline closely, above it at 2×2{\times}, 6×6{\times}, and 8×8{\times} and 0.0050.005 below it at 4×4{\times}, since Plücker camera conditioning already supplies the recall signal that KV-cache content provides on MG2, leaving no room for canonical averaging to add. WorldTrace-Landmark improves over sliding-window retention from 4×4{\times} onward (+8.9%+8.9\%, +14.1%+14.1\%, +7.3%+7.3\% at 4×4{\times}/6×6{\times}/8×8{\times}), with no significant gain at 2×2{\times} (−0.006-0.006 absolute, p>0.1p{>}0.1), since verbatim key injection provides a complementary recall signal that strengthens as camera-pose priors alone become insufficient at longer horizons.

E.5 Slot Allocation

Summary/recent split sensitivity.

The main experiments use Ns=4\smash{N_{s}}{=}4 summary slots and Nr=2\smash{N_{r}}{=}2 recent-window slots (total Ns+Nr=6\smash{N_{s}}{+}\smash{N_{r}}{=}6, matching the training context size). To test sensitivity to this split, we swept five allocations (Ns+Nr=6\smash{N_{s}}{+}\smash{N_{r}}{=}6, ABA loops at N=32N{=}32 and N=64N{=}64). Results are in Tab. 12. Ns≤2\smash{N_{s}}{\leq}2 collapses toward the sliding-window baseline, since with one slot the B→\toA detector overwrites the scene-A landmark. With two slots the B-side traversal evicts it before the return. Ns=3\smash{N_{s}}{=}3 is intermediate (0.6520.652/0.6930.693 at N=32N{=}32/6464) but still evicts the landmark. Ns=4\smash{N_{s}}{=}4 retains the landmark through the B-side return. Ns=5\smash{N_{s}}{=}5 adds only +0.009+0.009/+0.005+0.005, confirming a four-slot plateau.

E.6 Memory Accounting

WorldTrace never holds a full-attention KV cache. At every step the model attends over the same Ns+Nr\smash{N_{s}}{+}\smash{N_{r}} entries, so attention cost is constant per step and peak GPU memory is nearly flat in the rollout length. What a summary slot stores does evolve as generation proceeds, since each chunk that leaves the recent window updates the slot it belongs to, while the query position affects only the in-distribution slot-rank offset at which the slot is read through a single O⁡(1)O(1) rotation.

We report peak GPU memory at N=64N{=}64, 256256, and 512512 in Tab. 13. WorldTrace-Field matches the sliding-window baseline exactly at all three horizons because it adds nothing to the GPU-resident cache. Its recompute writer instead offloads the canonical key of each frame that leaves the recent window to host memory, which grows by 5.45.4 MB per generated latent frame and stays off the GPU. WorldTrace-Landmark keeps no history at all beyond the frozen scene-entry keys in its slots and adds a constant scene-anchor overhead of about 0.60.6 GB over the baseline at every horizon.

E.7 Streaming Summary Writer

The content writer of WorldTrace-Field is a recompute writer, which retains evicted canonical keys and recomputes each slot mean when group boundaries move. A strictly streaming alternative keeps one running sum and count per slot instead. Each evicted frame is folded into its slot once and then discarded, and a boundary shift is handled by an exact merge of adjacent buckets, so the writer state is O⁡(Ns)O(\smash{N_{s}}) and constant in rollout length.

We compare the two writers at N=32N{=}32 and N=48N{=}48 in Tab. 14. The streaming writer keeps most of the recompute writer’s coherence gain and reaches the lowest Scene Drift at N=32N{=}32, and both writers stay above the sliding-window baseline at both horizons. Since the streaming writer retains no history outside the cache, this comparison isolates the effect of the slot-rank positions of Def. 1 from any benefit of the extra statistics the recompute writer happens to keep.

Appendix F LoopBench: Loop Memory Benchmark

We propose LoopBench, a benchmark for episodic memory in autoregressive world models. Each task is a navigation path that departs from a location, visits other locations, and returns. The frames generated on the first visit serve as the reference, and we measure how closely the frames generated on the return reproduce them. LoopBench therefore needs no external reference video, as the rollout itself produces both the target and the prediction. Four properties of the path control task difficulty. (1) Waypoint count (KK): the number of intermediate locations between departure and return to A (ABA: K=1K{=}1, ABCDA: K=3K{=}3). (2) Rollout length (NN): the total number of AR chunks in the path. Longer rollouts put more chunks between the first visit and the return, so the revisited scene sits deeper in the compressed cache. (3) Camera orientation: the agent stays at A while the camera pans away by 90∘90^{\circ}, 180∘180^{\circ}, or 360∘360^{\circ} and then returns, testing whether the initial view is recalled after the pan. (4) Multi-revisit depth (RR): the number of times the repeated waypoint is visited in one path (ABABA returns to A twice, ABCBA and ABCDBA pass through B twice). Each axis varies one property while the others stay unchanged, following the principle that benchmark tasks should be picked to produce distinguishable rankings between candidate systems [58]. We show all twelve configurations in Fig. 8 and evaluate every one of them in Tab. 3. We show qualitative reconstructions on the ABA (axis 1) and pan 90∘90^{\circ} (axis 3) settings in Fig. 9 and Fig. 10.

Appendix G Implementation Details

G.1 Model Architecture and Self-Forcing Background

We evaluate on MG2-1.3B [32], a 1.3B-parameter autoregressive video world model based on Wan 1.3B T2V [87], with 30 transformer layers, 12 attention heads, and a head dimension of 128. Video is generated in AR chunks of 3 latent frames at latent resolution 44×8044\times 80 (352×640352\times 640 pixels), giving 880 tokens per latent frame. Each new chunk is denoised by a distilled flow-matching sampler conditioned on the KV cache of prior chunks. The model is trained with Self-Forcing [38], which rolls out on the student’s own KV cache rather than on teacher-forced context (related training schemes include Diffusion Forcing [10], CausVid [109], and one-step diffusion distillation [76]). Attention is restricted to a local window of local_attn_size=6=6 latent frames, so cross-frame temporal offsets stay ≤Δ​ttrain=5\leq\smash{\Delta t_{\mathrm{train}}}{=}5. At inference the rolling KV cache would grow without bound. Our method keeps it at the constant Lattn\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}}-latent-frame budget of the sliding window, which comes to 6×880×12×(128×2)×30×2≈0.976\times 880\times 12\times(128{\times}2)\times 30\times 2\approx 0.97 GB in fp16 per generated video at batch size 1 (880880 tokens/frame, 1212 heads, head dim 128128, ×2\times 2 for K and V, 3030 layers, 22 B per value), independent of generation length. The long-horizon failure is therefore not one of missing memories, since keys are stored verbatim and the model was simply never trained to read them through the temporal RoPE rotations they accumulate beyond Δ​ttrain\smash{\Delta t_{\mathrm{train}}} (App. C).

G.2 WorldTrace Algorithm and Baselines

WorldTrace cache update.

After each new chunk is generated, its keys and values enter the verbatim recent window. When the recent window exceeds Nr\smash{N_{r}} chunks, the oldest chunk is evicted and folded into the summary cache, by canonical key averaging over its temporal group (WorldTrace-Field, Eq. (3)) or by storing it as a canonical landmark when a scene entry is detected (WorldTrace-Landmark, Eq. (4)). We list these update steps in Alg. 1, together with the shared final step that re-rotates each canonical summary key to its virtual position when attention scores are computed.

Contrast with MG3.

Matrix-Game-3 [92] addresses long-horizon memory from the training side. It retrains a bidirectional diffusion backbone whose memory is built in during training, so that past frames are retrieved by camera pose and field-of-view overlap, injected as additional conditioning latents alongside the recent history, and learned through error-aware training and a modified temporal RoPE, followed by multi-segment distillation for real-time inference. We do not compare against MG3 because its memory is trained into the generator rather than implemented in the cache. There is no fixed pretrained checkpoint whose cache read/write WorldTrace could modify, so the comparison would conflate a retrained memory mechanism with our training-free, inference-time setting.

G.3 Hyperparameters, Compute, and Evaluation Protocol

Camera trajectory for the coherence qualitative panel.

The qualitative comparison in Fig. 4 (Sec. 4.2) is generated along a single camera path on Matrix-Game 2, played out over N=48N{=}48 AR chunks (∼57{\sim}57 s of decoded video). We show that path from a bird’s-eye view in Fig. 11, where the camera follows one continuous trajectory from the initial scene (start, n=1n{=}1) to a distinct end pose (n=48n{=}48), and the marked chunks n∈{8,18,24,32,40}n\in\{8,18,24,32,40\} give the waypoints shown as columns in Fig. 4. All methods in Fig. 4 follow this same trajectory.

Inference hyperparameters.

MG2-1.3B [32] uses 3 distilled denoising steps (t∈{1000,666,333}t\in\{1000,666,333\} with timestep shift 5.05.0), no classifier-free guidance at inference, a single conditioning image, and F=3F{=}3 latent frames per AR chunk. Each chunk is additionally conditioned on per-frame keyboard and mouse actions through the model’s action module, which is how the camera trajectories are controlled. In our setting, the first chunk is generated with an empty KV cache, and every later chunk attends to the accumulated compressed cache.

WorldTrace-Field hyperparameters.

Short-horizon experiments (N=8N{=}8) use Ns=2\smash{N_{s}}{=}2 summary slots and Nr=4\smash{N_{r}}{=}4 recent-window slots (Ns+Nr=Lattn=6\smash{N_{s}}+\smash{N_{r}}=\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}}{=}6). Longer horizon, LoopBench, and ablation experiments (Secs. 4.3–4.4) use Ns=4\smash{N_{s}}{=}4, Nr=2\smash{N_{r}}{=}2 (same total capacity) for both WorldTrace-Field and WorldTrace-Landmark. Compression uses uniform temporal grouping, splitting the T−NrT{-}\smash{N_{r}} frames outside the recent window into Ns\smash{N_{s}} equal groups. Each group’s keys are unrotated to canonical space, averaged, and re-rotated at the virtual position.

Evaluation protocol.

Each method is evaluated on 100100 videos generated from distinct initial frames. Multi-seed experiments use seeds {0,42,123,456,789}\{0,42,123,456,789\}. All experiments run on a single NVIDIA A100 80 GB GPU.

Compute.

WorldTrace-Field generates at ∼0.9{\sim}0.9 s per AR chunk at batch size 1, and VAE decode adds ∼2.5{\sim}2.5 s per chunk. The full experiment set required approximately 100 GPU-hours on single A100 80 GB GPUs. We report wall-clock time per AR chunk on one A100 80 GB at batch size 1 in Tab. 15. All methods stay within 6% of the sliding-window baseline, since the forward pass dominates the cache update, so the overhead of WorldTrace is negligible in practice.

Appendix H Discussion

H.1 Limitations

WorldTrace operates entirely at inference time, leaving the pretrained weights frozen and changing only what information the fixed-size KV cache retains (compressed summaries in place of evicted frames) and the virtual RoPE positions at which those entries are read, with the goal of improving long-horizon memory. Everything else, including per-chunk visual quality, motion dynamics, and action following, is inherited unchanged from the pretrained backbone. The method also assumes an autoregressive generator with temporal RoPE applied to keys and a known local attention window. Compression into a fixed budget of Ns\smash{N_{s}} slots is lossy by construction, since each WorldTrace-Field slot averages roughly T/NsT/\smash{N_{s}} frames, a ratio that grows with horizon, so frame-level detail inside a group is progressively blurred. Under WorldTrace-Landmark, a scene can be recalled later only if the scene-entry detector stored it as a landmark. Moreover, the cache holds only Ns\smash{N_{s}} landmarks, so a rollout that enters more scenes than that loses the oldest ones and can reliably revisit at most Ns\smash{N_{s}} distinct places. Future work could relax this cap, for example by merging evicted landmarks into a coarse residual summary slot so that discarded scenes leave a recoverable trace, or by selecting which landmark to evict based on predicted revisit likelihood.

H.2 Future Directions

Geometry-aware canonical keys.

Coupling the unrotate/rerotate primitive with camera-pose warping (\egthe Plücker and Warped-RoPE writers of MosaicMem [111] and UCM [104]) would align frames to a shared scene coordinate system and then average, so each summary token blends observations of similar scene content.

Learned scene-entry policies.

A small policy trained on action discontinuities, agent-pose changes, or scene-segmentation logits could let WorldTrace-Landmark commit landmarks during continuous motion and decide which landmark to select. The fixed split between Ns\smash{N_{s}} and Nr\smash{N_{r}} could become an autotunable schedule and adapt per backbone or horizon without the sweep of App. E.5.

Fine-tuning extensions.

WorldTrace stays within the attention window Lattn\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}}, where the budget Ns+Nr=Lattn\smash{N_{s}}+\smash{N_{r}}=\smash{L_{\mathrm{attn}}} keeps every summary slot in-distribution. Two light fine-tuning paths relax this budget. (i) Context-extension fine-tuning on synthetic long rollouts would let WorldTrace allocate more recent slots for coherence or more summary slots for longer recall at the same in-distribution cost. (ii) Position-aware fine-tuning that trains the model on the slot-rank offsets of Eq. (2) would tighten the canonical-mean approximation of WorldTrace-Field.

Training memory policies from revisit supervision.

The memory policy that decides what to store, compress, and evict could itself be trained, and revisit tasks supply the training signal for free, since whether the model reproduces the original scene on its return is directly measurable. Closed-loop simulators can collect such revisit episodes at scale, supporting supervised fine-tuning on rollouts where recall succeeds as well as reinforcement learning with the revisit score as reward. In both cases the backbone stays frozen and WorldTrace keeps every stored summary in-distribution, so only the lightweight policy over the cache is trained.

Scaling LoopBench.

We propose LoopBench (App. F) with four difficulty tiers, and it can grow beyond them, since longer paths, more waypoints, and richer camera trajectories are all generated by the same recipe, and evaluating other world models on it would show how well their memory mechanisms support revisits, complementing WorldScore [21], MIND [106], and VBench-2.0 [118].

H.3 Broader Impact

WorldTrace is an inference-time cache mechanism that alters no training data, modifies no weights, and expands none of the generative capabilities of the underlying video model, so the relevant considerations are those already attached to pretrained video world models. By keeping long-horizon generation within a constant memory budget, it also lowers the compute cost of building on pretrained generators, a cost that shapes the wider ecosystem reusing them, from score-distilled 3D synthesis [59, 101] with compute-aware gradient estimators [5, 72] to LLM-conditioned mesh generation [90] and motion attribution for video models [96]. We release no new datasets, and downstream use should follow the base models’ content policies.
